entries.meaning: Violent strife or open fighting; a riot or quarrel, not specifically a rebellion against authority.
befitting, suitable to; here, ornaments appropriate to dignified old age
Juliet's hot-tempered cousin, nephew of Lady Capulet; his name recalls Tybert, the cat in the Reynard the Fox tales.
A lady or woman, especially one admired or courted; not implying an illicit relationship.
estimation or counting of worth; she may be counted among the many but will not stand out as notable (playing on the saying that one is no number)
Form of address used to a servant or social inferior, often commanding: you there, fellow.
Exclamation of impatient dismissal: nonsense, come now.
Give (shortened form); God give you good evening is a greeting.
Italian title of respect for a gentleman: Sir, Mister.
A count invited to the Capulets' feast; one of the guests named on the invitation list, otherwise unmentioned in the play.
A deceased Veronese gentleman whose widow is on Capulet's guest list; he appears nowhere else in the play.
Italian title of respect for a gentleman: Sir, Mister.
A gentleman of Verona named on Capulet's guest list; he does not appear in the play.
Capulet's niece, the young woman Romeo is in love with before he meets Juliet; she never appears on stage.
Italian title of respect for a gentleman: Sir, Mister.
A gentleman named on Capulet's guest list; he does not appear in the play.
A guest named on Capulet's invitation list; he never appears in the play.
Capulet's niece, the young woman Romeo is in love with before he meets Juliet; she never appears on stage.
Lammas Day, 1 August, an English harvest festival; its Eve is 31 July.
The Nurse's own daughter, born about the same time as Juliet, who has died.
The Nurse's own daughter, born about the same time as Juliet, who has died.
Lammas Day, 1 August, an English harvest festival; its Eve is 31 July.
A dovecote: a building or structure where pigeons or doves are kept and bred.
The dovecote (a building housing pigeons), imagined as saying Shake as it trembled in the earthquake.
Holiness or sacred relic (popularly linked to 'Our Lady'); used in a mild oath, like 'by all that's holy'.
Stopped crying; ceased.
Stop, leave off (talking); cease.
Stab or wound in return; with a bawdy double sense of sexual penetration.
In return for its stabbing you; repay love's wounding in kind (with a bawdy pun on sexual thrusting).
A mask worn over the face; here Mercutio jokes that he puts a mask over a face already as ugly as a mask.
Part of the proverbial phrase 'candle-holder': one who merely holds the light for others, i.e. an onlooker rather than a participant.
Exclamation of impatient dismissal: nonsense, come now.
Tiny creatures or specks; minute beings so small as to be barely visible, like motes of dust.
Curtsies; bows or bends of the knee made as a mark of respect at court.
Queen Mab, in folklore a tiny fairy who delivers dreams to sleepers and plays mischievous tricks.
Queen Mab, in folklore a tiny fairy who delivers dreams to sleepers and plays mischievous tricks.
tangled, matted knots of hair, popularly believed to be made by mischievous elves or fairies during the night
Name of a servant in the Capulet household; a comic nickname meaning a cooking pot, suited to a kitchen servant.
Name of a servant in the Capulet household; a comic nickname meaning a cooking pot, suited to a kitchen servant.
A mask worn over the face, as by guests at a masked ball.
Familiar form of address to a man, here used casually to himself or a companion: my good fellow.
An acquaintance of Capulet's, otherwise unknown, whose wedding some twenty-five years earlier is used to date the last masked dance.
Festive celebration or ceremonial occasion; here, the Capulets' feast.
Festive celebration or ceremonial occasion; here, the Capulets' feast.
befitting, suitable; with 'ill', unsuitable or unbecoming
Familiar form of address to a man, here used casually to himself or a companion: my good fellow.
Faith; used in the mild oath "by my faith," meaning truly or indeed.
A Veronese gentleman, father of one of the departing guests at Capulet's feast; mentioned only here.
Moderating or softening; making hardships bearable by mixing them with something pleasant.
crept away secretly; slipped off quietly (here with reflexive 'him', meaning himself).
call up a spirit by magic spells and invocations
call up (a spirit or the dead) by magic spells
solemnly command a spirit to appear, invoking sacred or powerful names
Belonging to Rosaline, the young woman Romeo was infatuated with before meeting Juliet; she never appears on stage.
The woman a man loves and courts; his sweetheart or lady-love, with no sense of an illicit affair.
The woman a man loves and courts; his sweetheart or lady-love, with no sense of an illicit affair.
use magic invocations to call up a spirit (with a bawdy double meaning)
A small brown apple-like fruit eaten when half-rotten; its split shape made it slang for the female genitals.
The woman a man loves and courts; his sweetheart or lady-love, with no sense of an illicit affair.
Part of open-arse: slang name for the medlar fruit, from its split shape, used as a bawdy image of the female genitals.
Jesters or clowns, whose costumes were often green and yellow; also suggests silly people who foolishly stay virgins.
An exclamation of regret or sorrow; alas.
Behaviour, conduct; here, how she has acted, which he may think frivolous or too forward.
Afraid; fearful.
Belonging to a falconer, a person who trains and flies hawks and calls them back to the hand.
Belonging to a playful, spoiled child; a capricious youngster who toys with a pet bird on a string.
Latin for 'bless you'; a priest's greeting or blessing, here a surprised exclamation at the early visitor.
Not crammed with worries or cares; untroubled, free of burdens.
Disturbance or disorder of mind or body; an upset that prevents rest.
Spiritual; concerned with the soul, as a priest or confessor is.
favour or kindness; here, she returns his favour with her own
Formal rules of etiquette and ceremony, here the precise conventions of fashionable dueling.
Backhanded (in fencing); punto reverso is a backhanded thrust, an Italian fencing term Mercutio mocks as affected jargon.
Affected, fantastical fops; extravagant dandies full of fanciful airs and fashionable mannerisms.
Grandfather; here a jocular address to an old man, mocking Benvolio as if he were an old-fashioned elder complaining about the young.
Worthless, good-for-nothing women; low, contemptible creatures.
Italian title of respect for a gentleman: Sir, Mister; used here with mock formality.
French for good day; a mocking greeting, matching Romeo's fashionable French-style baggy breeches.
Comic misuse for invite, mocking the Nurse's blunder of confidence for conference; properly it means to write or compose.
A woman who runs a brothel or procures women for sex; a go-between in illicit affairs. Mercutio also puns on a dialect word for hare.
A woman who runs a brothel or procures women for sex; a go-between in illicit affairs. Mercutio also puns on a dialect word for hare.
Mouldy, grey with mould; with a pun on whore (hare was slang for prostitute).
Grey-haired with age, or grey with mould; punning on whore.
Grey-haired with age, or grey with mould; punning on whore.
Mouldy, grey with mould; punning on whore.
Roguery; knavish or impudent joking, the sort of talk deserving the hangman's rope (the Nurse's muddled word).
Part of 'skains-mates': disreputable companions, cutthroat cronies or loose women; 'skain' possibly from skean, a dagger. The exact sense is uncertain.
Dark and gloomy-looking, as under threatening clouds; frowning.
passion and vigour, thought of as carried in the blood
verbal decoration or embellishment; fine words as opposed to real substance
The Capulets, Juliet's family and their followers; a shortened form of the name.
out of doors; out and about in the streets.
hot temper; violent passions, thought of as stirred up in the blood
Keep company with, associate with; Mercutio puns on consort as a band of hired musicians.
Keep company with; Mercutio puns on the sense of a band of hired musicians playing together.
A violin bow; used jokingly here for his sword, continuing the pun on minstrels.
Keep company with, scornfully repeated, with a play on the sense of a band of hired musicians.
Italian for 'at the'; with the next word, a fencing term meaning 'the thrust', used scornfully of Tybalt, who fights in the fashionable Italian style.
Italian fencing term for a thrust; Mercutio mockingly names Tybalt by his fashionable fencing style ("the thrust wins the day").
Taunting insult: one who catches rats, like a cat; mocks Tybalt's name, which recalls Tibert, the cat in old fables.
Mildness or gentleness; merciful restraint (here, the restraint shown out of regard for Tybalt as a kinsman).
Guide or leader; that which directs one's actions.
Between.
fight, violent quarrel; here the street brawl itself
blood relation, kinsman (here Mercutio, the Prince's relative)
In Greek myth, son of the sun god Helios (Phoebus) who drove his father's sun-chariot recklessly, losing control of the horses.
Not gossiped about; unmentioned by others.
confident and unashamed, no longer shy or timid
An exclamation of grief or dismay: alas, woe is me (literally, woe the day).
Corpse; dead body.
Bankrupt; one who has lost everything and is utterly ruined.
Part of aqua vitae, literally water of life: strong distilled liquor such as brandy, taken as a restorative.
befitting, proper; with 'ill', unnatural or unbecoming
balanced, well-regulated; blended in proper proportion so as to be calm and self-controlled.
one's origin: the fact of being born, and the family and rank one is born into
one's origin: the fact of being born, and the family and rank one is born into
something that adorns and gives grace to; here, the intellect that should grace one's body and love
Lacking skill or training; inexperienced and clumsy.
A mild oath, roughly 'upon my life' or 'goodness me' (short for 'before me', i.e. as God is before me).
City in northern Italy, about 25 miles south of Verona, where Romeo goes in exile.
captured; arrested
City in northern Italy, about 25 miles south of Verona, where Romeo goes in exile.
A small draught of liquid, here a dose of poison.
Capsize, overturn (like a boat in a storm).
belonging to a crony or chatty female friend; the bowl is the punch bowl shared at women's social gatherings, such as christening feasts.
Descended from a family line; of noble lineage (some editions read 'allied', meaning connected by kinship or marriage).
An exclamation of grief or dismay; alas.
it would be (contraction of 'it were', subjunctive); here, it would be just as good if he were dead
Curse; a mild imprecation meaning may evil befall (them).
Speak badly of; disparage or criticize.
Between.
used for storing the bones or bodies of the dead; a charnel house is a vault where old bones dug from graves were piled.
City in northern Italy, about 25 miles south of Verona, where Romeo goes in exile.
City in northern Italy, about 25 miles south of Verona, where Romeo goes in exile.
Form of address used to a servant or social inferior, often commanding: you there, fellow.
Prayers.
Wholesome; healthy, fresh and good to breathe.
An exclamation of fear or dismay; alas.
An exclamation of fear or dismay; alas.
Woman (literally a woman's hooded head-covering, used jokingly for the wearer); a jealous hood is a jealous wife.
Woman (literally a woman's hooded head-covering, used jokingly for the wearer); a jealous hood is a jealous wife.
Form of address used to a servant or social inferior, often commanding: you there, fellow.
Respectful form of address to a young lady of the house, like Miss or my lady.
An exclamation of grief or dismay: alas, woe is me (literally, woe the day).
Part of aqua vitae, literally water of life: strong distilled liquor such as brandy, used to revive someone who has fainted.
An exclamation of grief; alas (with 'the day': woe to this day, what a dreadful day).
An exclamation of grief; alas (with 'the day': woe to this day, what a dreadful day).
robbed of her virginity; also punning on a flower stripped of its bloom.
An exclamation of grief or sorrow; alas.
Corpse; dead body.
Corpse; dead body.
Frown, look dark and threatening; show displeasure.
Hard, unyielding, merciless (of wit), punning on the dagger's metal.
Comic name Peter gives a musician; a rebeck was a three-stringed fiddle, so the surname mocks his instrument.
Comic surname for a musician, from the rebec, a medieval three-stringed fiddle played with a bow.
Comic name for a musician, from the small wooden peg inside a violin that supports the bridge and carries sound to the body.
Strong, coarse twine used for tying up bundles and parcels.
City in northern Italy, about 25 miles south of Verona, where Romeo goes in exile.

City in northern Italy, about 25 miles south of Verona, where Romeo goes in exile.
An iron bar used for prying something open; a crowbar.
Threat; menacing warning or denunciation.
Family burial vault or tomb.

Perhaps; by chance.
Family burial vault or tomb.
gone to the wrong place; strayed from where it belongs (its sheath on Romeo's belt).
secret, clandestine; done without others' knowledge.
